idea.t: Box the king in with your queen. Squeeze it to the edge. Then bring your king, and mate. The queen can't mate alone: your king has to help.
Put your queen a knight's jump from their king. Its row and its file fence the king into one part of the board. From there the king can never attack the queen.
Each time the king steps, put the queen a knight's jump away again. Every such move makes the box smaller. Don't give check: checks let the king out.
Once the king is on the edge with two squares left, stop squeezing. One more square taken is stalemate, and only a draw.
Walk your king over while theirs steps between its two squares. Head for one of the squares a knight's jump from their corner.
Mate comes with the queen next to their king, guarded by yours. Or along the edge, with your king facing theirs.
Before every queen move, ask: will their king still have a move, or is it check? If neither, it is stalemate.
Your rook cuts the king off along a row. Your king walks up to face theirs. Then a check pushes it back one row. Again and again, until the check on the edge is mate.
The rook holds a row their king can't cross. Keep the rook far from their king so it can't be attacked.
Walk your king up the board on your side of the rook's row, straight toward their king.

idea.h: 3. Check when the kings face each other
idea.t: Kings face to face with one square between: now check along the row. Their king has to step back.
If the kings aren't facing, don't check. Move the rook along its row, out of their king's reach. Their king has to step, and soon the kings face each other.
On the edge with the kings face to face, the check on the last row is mate.
One rook holds a row. The other checks on the next row up. The king steps back, and the rooks take turns.
When their king comes at a rook, move that rook to the far end of its row and carry on.
When the king reaches the edge, the next check mates. Your own king isn't needed.
Side by side, the two bishops cover two diagonals their king can't cross. Together they fence it like a rook.
Two bishops can't mate alone. Bring your king up close: it takes the squares the bishops can't reach.
Push the king into a corner. Then one bishop takes the last free square and the other checks.
In the corner their king has no square left. A quiet move now (red) is stalemate. Give check (green), and it is mate.
The mate only works in a corner of your bishop's colour. A light bishop mates in the two light corners.
If the king runs to the wrong corner, push it along the edge to the right one. The knight goes round in a W while your king and bishop keep it boxed.
Your king in front, the knight guarding the square next to the corner, and the bishop checks along the diagonal.
A king behind its own pawns has no square. A rook check on the last row mates.
One pawn step gives your king a square. Make it before your rook leaves the back row.
The king is walled in by its own pieces. A knight check is mate.

idea.h: Give the queen to close the wall
idea.t: The queen checks on the corner square. The rook has to take it, and the knight mates.
The knight takes the squares beside the king, its own pawn the one in front. A rook check down the edge mates.
The queen takes the pawn in front of the king with check. When the king takes back, the rook mates.
The rook checks next to the cornered king. The knight guards it and takes the other square.
With the rook on the seventh row, the knight step leaves the king no square. The rook mates next.
The rook checks beside the king, the knight guards the rook, and the pawn guards the knight.
A rook check next to the king on the edge, guarded by your king. The knight takes the squares on both sides.
Two bishops on crossing diagonals. The king's own rook and knight block it in.
Give the queen on the pawn in front of the king. When a pawn takes it, the bishop mates.
One bishop checks down the long diagonal, the other takes the square next to the king.
A bishop on the long diagonal holds the corner. The other bishop checks next to the king, guarded by the knight.
The rook holds the file next to the cornered king, its own pawn blocks the rest, and the bishop checks.
The rook takes next to the king with check. Once the king is in the corner, the rook steps aside and the bishop mates.
The bishop takes the square in front of the king, its own pawn blocks the other, and a rook mates on the edge.
The queen takes the pawn next to the king with check. After the king takes, the rook mates on that file.
A rook check on the back row, guarded by a bishop that also takes the square in front of the king.
The queen check makes the knight take it, and that opens the file for the rook.
The king's own rooks stand on both sides of it. A queen check from two squares in front mates.
The queen checks from a square touching the king's corner, guarded. The king's own pieces fill the squares it would run to.
A pawn guards the square next to the king. The queen goes there and mates.
A pawn deep in their camp guards the square in front of the king. The queen lands on it with mate.
The queen step threatens the mate, and nothing stops it.
The rook checks next to the king and the queen guards it from one square away on the diagonal: the king is boxed in.
Doubled on the seventh row, the rooks take the pawns in front of the king with check until it has no square.
King and pawn against a king wins only if your king gets ahead of its pawn. Push too soon and their king stands in front of it: a draw.
For a pawn on your half of the board, the key squares are the three squares two rows in front of it. Get your king onto one and the pawn queens, whoever is to move.
Kings face to face with one square between: the side to move has to give way. Step up so it is their move (green). The pawn push (red) lets their king stand in front of it.
When their king gives way to one side, step diagonally to the other. Your king lands on a key square.
Push the pawn only once your king stands on a key square. Then they walk up together: the king in front, the pawn behind it.

Picture a square with the pawn in one corner and the last row as its side. If your king can step into it, it catches the pawn. A pawn on its first square counts from the square in front, since it can jump two.
In front of the pawn, keep your king facing theirs with one square between. Then their king has to give way.
Here it is their move. Whatever their king does, yours steps to face it again. They never reach a key square.
Stay in front to the last row. With the pawn on the seventh and their king behind it, you are stalemated: a draw.
Kings on the same file with one square between are in opposition. Whoever has to move must give way. When it is their move, you have the opposition.
With three or five squares between the kings, the rule is the same: that is the distant opposition. Take it early and keep it as the kings come closer.

idea.h: Keep it as you close in
idea.t: When their king steps closer, step closer too and keep the kings facing. Don't push the pawn until your king stands on a key square.
A pawn on the edge can't be won if your king reaches the corner in front of it. Their king can't drive it out without stalemate.
Head straight for the corner in front of the pawn, or the squares beside it. Count: you need to get there before their king closes the door.
In the corner, step between the corner and the square next to it. If they push the pawn up close, you are stalemated.
With an edge pawn the stronger side wins only by shutting your king out of the corner, its king standing in front. Don't let it get there first.
Picture a square with the pawn in one corner and the last row as one side. A king that can step into it catches the pawn. A king outside it can't.

idea.h: Your game: count before you push
idea.t: Their pawn was slow: your king could catch it later. So the king came back to help your pawns first (green). The push you played (red) let their king take your pawns.
You had three pawns to two on the queenside. Your king had to walk over there (green) and eat their pawns. The pawn step you played (red) gave the win away.
Three pawns against three, all on the fifth row: push the middle one. Whichever pawn takes, push the other outside pawn. One of yours runs through.
It works when their king is too far to catch the pawn that gets through. Count before you give the first pawn away.
Here you want it to be their move: their king would have to give way. Your king has three squares where it is fine, theirs only two.
Walk round the three squares and come back. Their king has gone there and back on its two, and now it is their move in the same position.
The pawn push lets their king block it for good. Win the move first, then walk in.
Your king looks lost: too far from both pawns. Walk the diagonal: each step brings it closer to their pawn and to yours at the same time.
Going diagonally, a king covers as much ground towards two places as going straight. If they chase your pawn, you catch theirs. If they run, your pawn queens with your king beside it.
In pawn endings the king decides. Before you move, ask: which king reaches the pawns first? Can I take the opposition? Is there a waiting move?
Kings facing with one square between: whoever must move gives way. Take it to get in; take it to keep them out.
Count: if your king eats their pawns before theirs eats yours, and your pawn then queens first, go.
When the position would win if it were their move, lose a move with your king: walk a triangle, or make a spare pawn move.
A pawn move can't be taken back. Push when it breaks through, when it drags their king away, or when your pawn queens first.
A passed pawn on the edge pulls their king over. Your king then takes their other pawns.
Count the moves to queen for both sides. Then look one move further: does a new queen give check, or attack the other one?
A passed pawn far from the kings pulls their king away. While it chases the pawn, your king walks in and takes the pawns it left behind.
Push it until their king has to go after it. Then your king goes for their pawns on the other side.
A passed pawn guarded by a pawn ties their king to it for good. Their king can't take it, and can't leave it.
So your king can walk to the other side and take their pawns there.
Two pawns side by side, far from their king, can beat a rook. Push the front one first and keep them together so they guard each other.
On the sixth row, two connected pawns beat a lone rook. With their king close, the rook usually wins them.
Your rook behind your passed pawn gets stronger with every push. Theirs in front of it only gets more stuck.
Rooks go behind passed pawns: behind yours to push it, behind theirs to stop it.
Your king in front of your pawn on the seventh, their king cut off, their rook checking from the side. First push their king one file further with a check.
Before your king walks out, put the rook on the fourth row. That is where it will block the checks.
Walk your king out towards their rook. When the checks reach the rook's row, block with the rook: the bridge. The pawn queens.
Defending, with your king in front of their pawn, keep your rook on your third row. Their king can't come up without walking into checks.
Once their pawn steps onto your third row, your rook goes to the far end and checks from behind.
The pawn no longer shelters their king. From far behind the checks never run out.
Your rook on the file between the kings keeps their king away from your pawn. Then your king and pawn walk up together.
Cut off by two files or more, their king is usually too slow. Cut off by one, the defence often holds.
Against a rook in front of its edge pawn on the sixth, attack the pawn from the side. Keep your king near the other corner.
From the side, your rook guards the pawn's path and checks their king whenever it comes to help.
Your king goes to the short side of the pawn, the side nearer the edge. Your rook goes to the long side, far away.
From far away the rook checks from the side, and their king can't come close enough to stop the checks.
Use the rook to keep their king away from the pawn while yours comes back to take it.
If their king and pawn are far up the board and yours is far away, it may be a draw. A check that drives their king back gains the move you need.
On the seventh row your rook takes pawns from the side and keeps their king on its back row.
An active rook, attacking pawns or cutting the king off, is worth more than a pawn. A rook tied to guarding loses.
Rooks behind passed pawns. An active rook beats a passive one. Your king fights too: bring it up. Cut their king off from the pawns.
Ask: can my rook get behind a passed pawn, cut their king off, or attack a pawn? Can my king come closer? Find the move that does the most.
An edge pawn and a bishop that doesn't cover the queening square: if your king gets into that corner, it is a draw.
Count the race to the corner. Once you are in, shuffle in front of the pawn: nothing can drive you out.
The knight stops a pawn by guarding a square in front of it. Check first when their king would take that square.
Bring your king towards the pawn: once it guards the queening square, the knight is free.
A king stuck in front of its own edge pawn can be mated by a king and a knight. Box it in with your king first.
With their king trapped, the knight comes round and checks. Leave them a pawn move, or it is stalemate.

kinds.name: Bishops and knights: find the move

idea.t: A bishop is good against pawns on both wings. A knight is good when the pawns are on one side. Put your pawns on the other colour from your bishop.
Ask: can my king go in? Can a pawn run? Is there a square their piece can't guard?
Check and pin until their king has to stand in front of its pawn. Then bring your king one step closer.
Each time their king blocks its own pawn, your king gets a free move. Repeat until your king helps take the pawn.
With a bishop or rook pawn on the seventh, hide your king beside it. If their queen takes the pawn, it is stalemate.
It works only for the edge pawns and the pawns next to the bishops' files. Against the others, the queen wins.
Push their king to the edge, then look for a check that also hits the rook. A rook that strays from its king is lost.
Their rook will check and try to pin your king against your queen. Keep your king and queen on different lines.
Your king hides from checks near its pawns. A passed pawn is worth more than in any other ending. Check only when it gains something.
Look for checks that also attack something. Then look at theirs: can their queen give checks forever?

units.title: The queen mate
units.why: Four won endings ran out of time. A mate you can play without thinking saves the clock.

slides.t: Box the king in with your queen. Squeeze it to the edge. Then bring your king, and mate. The queen can't mate alone: your king has to help.
Put your queen a knight's jump from their king. Its row and its file fence the king into one part of the board. From there the king can never attack the queen.
Each time the king steps, put the queen a knight's jump away again. Every such move makes the box smaller. Don't give check: checks let the king out.
Once the king is on the edge with two squares left, stop squeezing. One more square taken is stalemate, and only a draw.
Walk your king over while theirs steps between its two squares. Head for one of the squares a knight's jump from their corner.
Mate comes with the queen next to their king, guarded by yours. Or along the edge, with your king facing theirs.
Before every queen move, ask: will their king still have a move, or is it check? If neither, it is stalemate.

units.title: Rook endings
units.why: Every rook ending with one pawn left heads for one of two positions.

slides.t: Your rook on the file between the kings keeps their king away from your pawn. Then your king and pawn walk up together.
Cut off by two files or more, their king is usually too slow. Cut off by one, the defence often holds.
Your king in front of your pawn on the seventh, their king cut off, their rook checking from the side. First push their king one file further with a check.
Before your king walks out, put the rook on the fourth row. That is where it will block the checks.
Walk your king out towards their rook. When the checks reach the rook's row, block with the rook: the bridge. The pawn queens.
Defending, with your king in front of their pawn, keep your rook on your third row. Their king can't come up without walking into checks.
Once their pawn steps onto your third row, your rook goes to the far end and checks from behind.
The pawn no longer shelters their king. From far behind the checks never run out.
Rooks go behind passed pawns: behind yours to push it, behind theirs to stop it.

slides.t: The mate only works in a corner of your bishop's colour. A light bishop mates in the two light corners.

units.title: Opposition and the edge pawn
units.why: Which king has to give way decides most pawn endings.

slides.t: Kings on the same file with one square between are in opposition. Whoever has to move must give way. When it is their move, you have the opposition.
With three or five squares between the kings, the rule is the same: that is the distant opposition. Take it early and keep it as the kings come closer.

slides.h: Keep it as you close in
slides.t: When their king steps closer, step closer too and keep the kings facing. Don't push the pawn until your king stands on a key square.

Picture a square with the pawn in one corner and the last row as its side. If your king can step into it, it catches the pawn. A pawn on its first square counts from the square in front, since it can jump two.
In front of the pawn, keep your king facing theirs with one square between. Then their king has to give way.
Here it is their move. Whatever their king does, yours steps to face it again. They never reach a key square.
Stay in front to the last row. With the pawn on the seventh and their king behind it, you are stalemated: a draw.
A pawn on the edge can't be won if your king reaches the corner in front of it. Their king can't drive it out without stalemate.
Head straight for the corner in front of the pawn, or the squares beside it. Count: you need to get there before their king closes the door.
In the corner, step between the corner and the square next to it. If they push the pawn up close, you are stalemated.
With an edge pawn the stronger side wins only by shutting your king out of the corner, its king standing in front. Don't let it get there first.
In pawn endings the king decides. Before you move, ask: which king reaches the pawns first? Can I take the opposition? Is there a waiting move?
Kings facing with one square between: whoever must move gives way. Take it to get in; take it to keep them out.
Count: if your king eats their pawns before theirs eats yours, and your pawn then queens first, go.

slides.t: Here you want it to be their move: their king would have to give way. Your king has three squares where it is fine, theirs only two.
Walk round the three squares and come back. Their king has gone there and back on its two, and now it is their move in the same position.
The pawn push lets their king block it for good. Win the move first, then walk in.
Your king looks lost: too far from both pawns. Walk the diagonal: each step brings it closer to their pawn and to yours at the same time.
Going diagonally, a king covers as much ground towards two places as going straight. If they chase your pawn, you catch theirs. If they run, your pawn queens with your king beside it.

slides.t: Against a rook in front of its edge pawn on the sixth, attack the pawn from the side. Keep your king near the other corner.
